explanation: Tolkien wrote it as one long novel. His publisher split it into three volumes in 1954 and 1955, largely because paper was scarce after the war and one huge book was costly.

claims.text: Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as one novel, not as a trilogy of three separate novels.
The Lord of the Rings was first published in three volumes in 1954 and 1955.
The publisher split the book into three volumes largely because of post-war paper shortages and the cost of one very long book.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Wikipedia gives economic reasons. It says the division was to minimize any potential financial loss due to the high cost of type-setting and modest anticipated sales. However, the sources I found do not directly say the paper shortage was the stated reason for splitting the book into three volumes. The explicit rationale is cost, mainly typesetting and printing, plus limited expected sales.

claimResults.note: Search 2 supports the cost half (high typesetting and printing costs, modest expected sales) but says the sources do not give a paper shortage as the reason for the split; the Tolkien Estate links scarce, costly paper only to the writing and production generally. The claim's 'largely because of post-war paper shortages' is not confirmed.

issues.note: c3 is left uncertain: the sources found give the publisher's reason for three volumes as cost (high typesetting and printing costs and modest expected sales), and none says paper scarcity drove the split. The explanation's 'largely because paper was scarce after the war' should be reworded to the cost reason, for example 'to keep the cost of one very long book down', and c3 restated to match.
